hub.faqTitle: Common questions about roll forming lines

faq.q: What does a roll forming line do?
faq.a: It passes coil sheet through a series of roll stations, forming it into the required profile step by step. Punching and cutting can also be done in line, giving uninterrupted production from coil to finished profile.

faq.q: What determines the price of a roll forming line?
faq.a: Four things drive it most: the complexity of the profile section (number of stations), sheet thickness and width, line speed, and the level of automation (punching station, flying shear, automatic stacking). That is why we do not publish catalogue prices — send your profile drawing and we will size the line and quote it.

faq.q: Can you produce a profile that is not in your catalogue?
faq.a: Yes. The roll set is designed from the profile drawing you send and manufactured in our own facility. The seven listed profile families are a starting point, not a limit.

faq.q: Can I run more than one profile on the same line?
faq.a: Yes, by changing the roll set. What matters here is changeover time: if you will run many section types, fast changeover directly affects utilisation, which in turn drives the line's payback.

faq.q: What is the roll forming process, step by step?
faq.a: Coil is loaded onto a decoiler, straightened to take out coil-set memory, then fed into the line by servo feeder. Where the profile needs holes or slots, punching stations work in line. The strip then passes through the roll forming machine, where each station bends it a little further until the section is complete, and cutting and stacking finish the cycle. Because the shape is reached gradually across many stations rather than in one press stroke, no heat is involved — which is why it is called cold roll forming.

faq.q: What is cold roll forming?
faq.a: Forming at room temperature. The strip is bent progressively by successive roll stations instead of being heated and pressed, so the surface finish and any coating survive the process — which matters for pre-painted and galvanised coil, the usual material for cable tray, solar and cladding profiles. Every line on this page is a cold roll forming line.

faq.q: What are the disadvantages of roll forming?
faq.a: Two, and they are worth knowing before committing. A roll set is made for one section, so each new profile means new tooling — roll forming rewards volume and repetition rather than one-off work. And the cross-section stays constant along the length; a part that changes shape along its run needs a different process. Where those two conditions are met, little else matches it for output per hour.

dilme.faqTitle: Common questions about coil slitting lines

faq.q: What does a coil slitting line do?
faq.a: It cuts a wide steel coil lengthwise into narrower strips of the width you need, then re-coils those strips. One master coil therefore yields several strips sized to your orders, which lowers both scrap and stock cost.

faq.q: Which capacity should I choose?
faq.a: The deciding factor is the maximum coil weight you will process. Light series are built for 1,500–4,000 kg and 0.5–2 mm sheet thickness; heavy series for 6,000–15,000 kg and 0.8–5 mm. Size for your volume 2–3 years out rather than today — the frame cannot be enlarged later.

faq.q: Should I buy a slitting line or a cut-to-length line?
faq.a: The difference is the shape of the output. A slitting line cuts the coil lengthwise and the output is still a coil — in narrow strips. A cut-to-length line cuts across the coil and the output is a flat sheet. Choose slitting if you sell strip, cut-to-length if you sell sheet to fixed dimensions. The two can also be combined in one line.

faq.q: What determines the price of a coil slitting line?
faq.a: Four things drive it most: coil weight capacity, the sheet thickness range, how many strips are cut at once, and the level of automation (loading car, automatic setsquare, recoiler tension control). That is why we quote per project rather than from a catalogue — send your coil weight, thickness and target strip dimensions and we will size it.

faq.q: How does commissioning work?
faq.a: The line is fully assembled and tested at our own facility before shipment, so on site only installation and commissioning remain. That keeps installation time short. Operator training is given during commissioning.

faq.q: What is the difference between cutting and slitting?
faq.a: Slitting cuts along the length of the coil and produces narrower coils. Cutting, in the cut-to-length sense, cuts across it and produces flat sheets. Slitting leaves you with coil to feed another process; cut-to-length leaves you with finished sheet.

faq.q: What are the different types of slitting line?
faq.a: The cutting principle does not change from one line to the next — circular knives on an arbor, set to the strip widths you need. What separates lines is capacity: coil weight, strip thickness, and how many strips one pass yields. The frame, the drive and the way strips are held under tension on the recoiler scale with those. Choosing between them comes back to your heaviest coil and thickest material — see the capacity question above.

highlights.title: Length accuracy
highlights.text: Servo feeding and encoder measurement cut sheet lengths within tight tolerances, with repeatability in serial production.

highlights.title: Clean cutting
highlights.text: The guillotine blade gap is set to the sheet thickness for burr-free, distortion-free cuts.

paras: Every unit, from the first link of the line to the final stack, comes from a single manufacturer: decoiler, straightener, feeder, shear and stacker are sized to each other. Compatibility problems seen in lines assembled from multiple suppliers are eliminated from the start.
Speed control uses Schneider Lexium and Altivar series drives; the line is fully assembled and tested at our factory before shipment, which keeps on-site commissioning short.
The line configuration is engineered to your sheet thickness, coil weight and sheet dimensions; if needed, it can be combined with a slitting unit to produce both strips and sheets.

faq.q: What does a cut-to-length line do?
faq.a: It uncoils, straightens and cuts the strip into flat sheets at the length you set. The output is not a coil but sheet to fixed dimensions. The line consists of a decoiler, straightener, servo feeder, guillotine shear and stacking unit.

faq.q: Should I buy a cut-to-length line or a slitting line?
faq.a: The difference is the shape of the output. A cut-to-length line cuts across the coil and produces flat sheet. A slitting line cuts lengthwise; the output is still a coil, in narrow strips. Choose cut-to-length if you sell sheet to fixed sizes, slitting if you sell strip. The two can be combined in one line.

faq.q: How is sheet flatness achieved?
faq.a: Coil-set memory is removed in the straightening unit, with roll pressures adjusted to the sheet thickness. The guillotine blade clearance is also set to thickness, so the cut is free of burrs and distortion. For sensitive surfaces, an optional PVC film unit protects the sheet from scratching before stacking.

faq.q: What determines the price?
faq.a: Coil weight capacity, sheet thickness and width, cutting accuracy and the level of automation (loading car, automatic stacking, PVC film) are the drivers. That is why we quote per project rather than from a catalogue.

faq.q: What is CTL in steel?
faq.a: CTL is shorthand for cut-to-length. A CTL line takes coil, straightens it and cuts it across into flat sheets at a set length. It is the opposite of a slitting line, which cuts along the coil and re-coils the narrower strips.

faq.q: What is the difference between blanking and cut-to-length?
faq.a: A cut-to-length line produces rectangular sheet at a set length — every piece the same simple shape. Blanking cuts a profiled outline, a contour defined by a die rather than just a length. If the part is rectangular, a cut-to-length line does it faster and with far less tooling; if it has a contour, it belongs on a press.

story: Servosteel was founded when a group of young engineers set out to build cost-effective and easy-to-control press feeding systems. We started with decoilers, straighteners and servo feeders; field experience gradually grew into complete line engineering — today we install coil slitting, cut-to-length and roll forming lines turnkey.

What sets us apart is that every link of the line is produced under one roof: mechanical design, manufacturing, automation software and commissioning are all in the same team. Our customers work with a single partner, and the line components arrive perfectly matched.
Lines built at our facility in Sancaktepe, Istanbul are producing today in more than 48 countries — across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Far East.

servo-vs-mekanik-besleme.name: Servo feeder or mechanical feeder?
servo-vs-mekanik-besleme.metaTitle: Servo Feeder vs Mechanical Feeder: Comparison
servo-vs-mekanik-besleme.metaDesc: Differences between servo feeding and mechanical/pneumatic feeders: accuracy, die change, speed and investment. Which is right for your job?
servo-vs-mekanik-besleme.hero: There are two ways to feed strip into a press line. The difference is not only price: part tolerance, die change time and line flexibility all change.

rows.label: Pitch accuracy
rows.a: Closed loop with servo motor and encoder; tolerance holds in series production
rows.b: Limited by mechanical cam or pneumatic stroke; pitch drifts with wear

rows.label: Changing the pitch
rows.a: Value entered on the panel, takes seconds
rows.b: Requires mechanical adjustment or a cam change

rows.label: Die change
rows.a: Recipe memory for up to 250 dies; no re-setup

rows.label: Press synchronization
rows.a: Fully synchronized via cam signal, pilot release standard
rows.b: Limited; synchronization gets harder at high stroke rates

rows.label: Investment and running cost
rows.a: Higher up front, lower scrap and downtime
rows.b: Lower up front, higher setup time and scrap

chooseA: Your part tolerance is tight and must hold across a production run
You change several dies within a shift
You use pilot pins or run at high stroke rates
servo-vs-mekanik-besleme.chooseBTitle: A mechanical feeder is enough if
chooseB: You run long series with a single die
Pitch tolerance is loose and surface is not critical
Budget constraints drive the initial investment
servo-vs-mekanik-besleme.verdict: As die variety grows, the setup and scrap savings of a servo feeder close the initial price gap. If you produce one part in long runs, a mechanical feeder is still a reasonable choice.

dilme-vs-boy-kesme.metaDesc: Slitting vs cut-to-length: output product, cutting direction, equipment and applications — which line fits your business?
dilme-vs-boy-kesme.hero: Both lines process coil, but they cut in different directions: one produces strip coils, the other flat sheets. Your output decides the line.

rows.label: Typical customer
rows.a: Roll forming, profile and tube producers
rows.b: Press shops, laser cutting and sheet fabricators

chooseA: Your output will be strip in coil form
You will feed the strips into your own roll forming or tube line
You want to split wide master coils into ordered widths
chooseB: Your output will be flat sheets at a defined length
The sheets will feed a press, laser or press brake
dilme-vs-boy-kesme.verdict: These are not alternatives to each other — they make different products. If you need both strip and sheet, let us discuss combined lines that do slitting and cut-to-length on one frame.

hidrolik-vs-mekanik-acici.name: Hydraulic or mechanical decoiler?
hidrolik-vs-mekanik-acici.metaDesc: Differences between hydraulic and mechanical decoilers: capacity, mandrel expansion, braking and loading. Which one suits your coil weight?
hidrolik-vs-mekanik-acici.hero: The difference is not just capacity: how the mandrel clamps, how the coil is braked and how it is loaded onto the shaft all change.

rows.label: Braking
rows.a: Hydraulic brake, controlled to line speed

rows.label: Coil loading
rows.a: Aligned with a hydraulic loading car
rows.b: Mounted on the shaft by forklift

rows.label: Operator effort
rows.b: High — manual clamping on every coil

chooseA: You change coils frequently during a shift
Your line speed is high and controlled braking is needed
chooseB: Your coils are under 2.5 tonnes and narrow
You need to keep the investment as low as possible
hidrolik-vs-mekanik-acici.verdict: With heavy coils and frequent changes, hydraulic pays for itself quickly through operator time and safety. For narrow strip and light coils, the mechanical series is still the most economical solution.

features.title: In-line punching
features.text: Ventilation and mounting holes are punched by servo punching stations on the line — no separate operation needed.

features.title: Fast size changeover
features.text: Recipe-based switching between different tray widths keeps setup times to a minimum.

features.title: Galvanized-sheet friendly
features.text: Rolls are machined and hardened to avoid damaging the zinc coating (4140 steel, 58-60 HRC).

process.title: Coil loading and decoiling
process.text: Cable tray is usually produced from pre-galvanized coil, and a tray line typically runs several widths from the same stock. That makes coil changing a routine event rather than an occasional one, which is why the decoiler and its loading arrangement have more effect on real output than the forming speed does.

process.title: Straightening
process.text: Coil set is removed before the strip is punched. A tray is a long shallow channel and it shows curvature clearly once formed; more practically, tray sections are bolted end to end along a run, so a member that is not straight makes every coupler in the run harder to fit.

process.title: Perforation and punching
process.text: Ventilation slots and the coupler holes at the ends are punched flat. Perforated tray exists for a reason — the openings let heat out of bundled cable and let the tray drain — so the pattern is a functional specification, not decoration. The punch is servo-fed so that the slot pattern and the end holes stay in the right relationship to the finished length.

process.title: Roll forming
process.text: The channel is formed across the stations. The detail that decides tray quality is the edge: the return flange along the top of each side is what makes a thin shallow channel stiff enough to span between supports, and it is also what cables are dragged across during installation. It is formed to a radius that keeps the section rigid without leaving an edge that damages cable insulation.

process.title: Cut to length in phase with the pattern
process.text: The cut is timed to the perforation, not just to the length counter. Every tray has to end with the same amount of solid material and the same coupler hole position at both ends, otherwise the joints along a run do not line up. A line that only counts length will make trays that measure correctly and still will not bolt together consistently.

process.title: Exit conveyor and stacking
process.text: Finished trays run out on a conveyor and are stacked. Tray nests inside itself, so stacking is normally what determines how much goes on a pallet and therefore what shipping costs — which for a low-value high-volume product is a bigger part of the delivered price than most buyers expect.

faq.q: Can I produce perforated and plain trays on the same line?
faq.a: Yes. The punching unit is integrated into the line; changing the recipe switches between perforated and plain tray. Hole pattern and pitch are tooled per order.

faq.q: How long does a size changeover take?
faq.a: Width is set by the cassette structure; the operator selects the size on the panel and the mechanical adjustment takes minutes. A height change may require swapping the roller set.

faq.q: Which sheet materials does it handle?
faq.a: Cold rolled, galvanized, aluminium and stainless steel. To protect the zinc coating, roller surfaces and pressure values are set according to the material.

faq.q: What is a cable tray roll forming machine?
faq.a: It is the roll forming machine at the heart of a cable tray production line: strip enters from a decoiler, is straightened and servo-fed, holes and slots are punched in line, and successive roll stations bend the sheet step by step into the tray section before cut-off and stacking. Because the section forms gradually and at room temperature, galvanized and pre-painted sheet keeps its coating — which is why trays are almost always produced from coated coil. On this page the machine is described as part of the complete line, since that is how it is supplied: one manufacturer, one control system, from coil to stacked tray.

faq.q: Why does the cut have to be phased to the perforation?
faq.a: Because cable tray is installed as a continuous run of bolted sections. Every piece needs the same solid margin and the same coupler hole position at each end, so that the joints repeat identically down the length of the installation. If the line simply counts length and cuts, the pieces will all measure the same and the perforation will creep relative to the ends, which shows up as couplers that do not line up. Phasing the shear to the punch is what prevents that, and it is a specific thing to ask about when comparing lines.

faq.q: What actually determines how stiff a tray is?
faq.a: The return flange along the top edge of each side, far more than the sheet thickness. A plain channel of the same thickness deflects a great deal more, because almost all the stiffness against bending comes from material at the extremes of the section. That is also why the perforation pattern stops short of the edges — perforating the flange takes out the material that is doing the work. If you are comparing trays on thickness alone you are comparing the wrong number.

faq.q: Does the edge form affect the cables?
faq.a: Yes, and it is a real installation issue rather than a theoretical one. Cables are pulled along a tray by hand over long runs, and an edge that is left sharp or has a burr from the forming or the shear will score insulation. The return flange is formed to a radius partly for stiffness and partly for this. It is worth looking at a sample piece from any supplier and running a hand along the inside edge — it tells you more about the line than a datasheet does.

faq.q: How much of the delivered cost is shipping?
faq.a: More than most buyers assume, which is why tray is usually made close to where it is used. It is a light, bulky, low-value product, so a container fills up long before it reaches its weight limit and the freight is being paid on air. Tray nests inside itself, so how well it stacks directly changes the landed cost. This is also the commercial reason a tray line is often the first roll forming investment for a contractor who was previously buying in — the transport saving alone can carry a large part of the case.

faq.q: Can the same line make ladder tray and wire mesh tray?
faq.a: No, and it is worth being clear about it early because the three products are often quoted together. Roll formed tray is a formed sheet channel. Ladder tray is two side rails with rungs welded across, so it needs a welding line rather than a forming line. Wire mesh tray is welded wire, which is a different process again. If your product range covers more than one of these, they are separate investments and should be planned as such.

solar-profil.name: Solar C-Profile Production Line
solar-profil.short: A high-speed roll forming solution for PV mounting profiles.
solar-profil.hero: A line producing hat, C and Omega profiles for solar power plant mounting structures directly from coil; punching stations open the mounting holes in-line, so profiles arrive on site ready to install.
solar-profil.meta: Solar mounting profile production line: a complete, high-speed roll forming line with punching stations for PV structure profiles.

features.title: Profile form to your project
features.text: Roll tooling is designed for hat, C, U or Omega sections according to the EPC's structural design.

features.title: Suitable for Magnelis® and galvanized
features.text: High-corrosion-resistant coated sheets are formed with roll surfaces that protect the coating.

features.title: Length and hole recipes
features.text: Hole patterns and lengths for different table types are selected as recipes on the HMI.

process.title: Coil loading and decoiling
process.text: Solar mounting profiles are almost always rolled from a coated coil — hot-dip galvanized or a zinc-aluminium-magnesium coating such as Magnelis. The coating is the corrosion protection for the whole 25-year life of the plant, so handling from the decoiler onward is set up to avoid scoring the surface rather than simply to move the strip.

process.title: Straightening
process.text: Coil set is taken out before punching. A solar table is an assembly of long slender members bolted to each other, and a purlin that arrives bowed does not just look wrong — it fights the installer at every bolt and puts the array out of plane, which shows up later as uneven module loading.

process.title: In-line punching
process.text: Mounting holes and slots are punched flat, before the section is formed. This is what lets the profile go straight from the truck to the structure with no drilling on site. The punch is servo-fed, so the hole pattern follows the recipe for that project rather than being set by mechanical stops that have to be re-adjusted every time the layout changes.

process.title: Roll forming
process.text: The hat, C or Omega section is built up across the stations. Coated material is the constraint here: the roller surfaces and pressures are set so the coating is not cracked or peeled at the tightest radii, because a bend that has broken the coating is a corrosion site that no amount of paint on site will fix properly.

process.title: Flying shear
process.text: The profile is cut on the move rather than stopping the line. On a solar job that matters more than it sounds — the order is thousands of pieces in a handful of lengths, and a line that has to decelerate and stop for every cut spends a large part of the shift not producing.

process.title: Automatic stacking
process.text: Finished profiles are collected and stacked in bundles ready for loading. Solar sites take delivery in large lots on a schedule, so consistent bundling is part of the product: bundles that match the erection sequence save the installer sorting a field full of similar-looking profiles.

faq.q: Can I produce both C and U profiles on the same line?
faq.a: Yes; with a cassette change, C, U and sigma sections run on the same frame. If you switch often, we recommend a quick-change cassette configuration.

faq.q: Are holes and slots punched inline?
faq.a: A hydraulic press unit is integrated into the line; mounting holes and adjustment slots are punched before the profile is cut — no second operation needed.

faq.q: Does hot-dip galvanized sheet suffer in forming?
faq.a: With roller surface and pressure matched to the coating, it stays intact. Our rollers are made from 4140 steel and hardened to 58-60 Rockwell.

faq.q: Why is the coating chosen before the profile is designed?
faq.a: Because it decides both the corrosion life and how the section can be formed. Hot-dip galvanized coil and zinc-aluminium-magnesium coatings such as Magnelis behave differently at a tight radius, and the coating also determines what happens at the cut ends and the punched holes, where bare steel is exposed. Zinc-aluminium-magnesium coatings are chosen partly because they give some self-healing at cut edges, which matters on a profile that is punched and sheared thousands of times. Tell us the coating with the drawing — the roller radii are set for it.

faq.q: Can holes be punched after forming instead?
faq.a: It is possible but it is the wrong way round for this product. Punching a formed section means punching through a curved or stiffened area, which distorts the profile locally and leaves a hole that is harder to control dimensionally. Punching flat keeps the pattern accurate and lets the whole thing be done in one pass through the line. The reason solar profiles are punched in line at all is to remove site drilling — doing it afterwards puts that cost straight back.

faq.q: What does a change in the mounting layout cost on the line?
faq.a: If it is a change in hole positions or lengths, it is a recipe change and no tooling is involved — that is what the punching stations and the length recipes are for, and it is why solar work suits this kind of line. If the profile section itself changes, that is a roller set question and a different conversation. Worth separating the two when you are planning: layout changes are routine, section changes are not.

faq.q: Does hot-dip galvanized sheet lose anything during forming?
faq.a: Not if the radii and pressures are right for it. Zinc coating is more brittle than the steel underneath, so damage shows up as fine cracking on the outside of the tightest bends rather than as visible peeling. That is a tooling design question, decided when the roller set is made rather than adjusted afterwards. It is also why sending the coating specification with the profile drawing is not a formality.

faq.q: Which sections are normally used for solar mounting structures?
faq.a: Hat, C and Omega sections cover most of it, in various depths depending on span and wind zone. The structural design is the plant designer's responsibility and it varies a great deal by country — snow and wind loading move the section size more than anything else. We tool to the section on your drawing; if the project is at an earlier stage than that, it is usually more productive to fix the structural design first and specify the line around it than the other way round.

agir-raf.name: Storage Rack Production Line
agir-raf.metaTitle: Storage Rack Roll Forming Machine for Racking
agir-raf.short: A punching-station line for rack uprights and beam profiles.
agir-raf.hero: A line producing the load-bearing rack uprights and beams of logistics warehouses; multi-row mounting holes are punched in-line by servo punches, and dimensional stability is maintained even in thick sheet.
agir-raf.meta: Storage rack production line: a custom roll forming solution with punching stations for rack uprights and beam profiles.

features.title: Multi-row punching
features.text: The hook holes of upright profiles are punched by servo stations without slowing the line down.

features.title: Thick sheet capability
features.text: Frame and roll sizing suited to the high wall thicknesses racking systems demand.

features.title: Dimensional repeatability
features.text: Servo feeding and encoder control keep hole-to-hole precision in serial production.

process.title: Coil loading and decoiling
process.text: Racking is normally rolled from pre-galvanized coil, so the strip arrives with its coating already on it. That governs how the coil is handled from the first metre: the decoiler and the guides are set so the surface is not dragged, because every scratch on a rack upright is a corrosion start point in a warehouse that will be washed down.

process.title: Straightening
process.text: Coil set is removed before punching rather than after. A strip that still holds curvature feeds unevenly through the punch, and any feed error there turns directly into a hole-position error — which is the one thing a rack profile cannot tolerate.

process.title: Multi-row punching
process.text: The connector holes are punched flat, in the pattern the rack system uses. The controlling number is not hole size but pitch accumulation: an upright carries connectors along its whole length, so a small repeated feed error adds up over a tall column. Servo feeding with encoder measurement keeps each hole referenced to the run, not just to the hole before it.

process.title: Roll forming the perforated strip
process.text: Forming a strip that is already perforated is not the same job as forming a solid one. The web is weaker at every hole, so the station sequence is laid out to bring the section up without pulling material across the openings — otherwise the holes deform into ovals and the connector no longer seats square.

process.title: Cut in phase with the hole pattern
process.text: The cut is not simply to length. It has to land in a fixed relationship to the perforation, so that the first and last holes sit where the rack design expects them on every single upright. A line that cuts to length alone will produce profiles that are the right size and still unusable.

process.title: Run-out and stacking
process.text: Finished profiles are collected and stacked. Uprights are long and relatively slender, so support spacing on the run-out matters: a profile allowed to sag under its own weight before it is stacked keeps some of that bow, and a bowed upright will not sit plumb in an assembled frame.

faq.q: Can uprights and beams run on the same line?
faq.a: Their sections differ, so two roller sets are normally needed. Depending on your order mix, a single frame carrying two sets can also be built.

faq.q: How is the hole pattern defined?
faq.a: It is tooled to the hook pitch of your rack system; pitch and hole shape are project specific. A sample or technical drawing is enough to match your existing system.

faq.q: What sheet thickness does the line handle?
faq.a: Heavy duty rack profiles typically call for thick material; the section and thickness range are sized per project. We define capacity together from your drawing.

faq.q: Which standards apply to racking, and what do they ask of the production line?
faq.a: Static pallet racking is designed to EN 15512, with EN 15620 covering manufacturing and installation tolerances and EN 15635 the operation and inspection of the installed system. Racking is a load-bearing structure, so what the line has to guarantee is dimensional: section geometry and hole position within the tolerance the design was calculated at. The design calculation and the CE responsibility belong to the rack system owner — the line has to be able to produce to it repeatably, day after day.

faq.q: Why does hole pitch accuracy matter more than hole size?
faq.a: Because pitch error accumulates and hole size does not. A hole slightly oversize is a local fit issue; a feed that is consistently a fraction of a millimetre long puts every hole progressively further out along the upright, and by the top of a tall column the connector will not go in. This is why the punching station is fed by servo with encoder measurement rather than by a mechanical stop, and why the specification you should compare between suppliers is pitch tolerance over the full profile length, not per step.

faq.q: Which material is used for rack profiles?
faq.a: Uprights and beams are usually rolled from structural steel in the S350GD to S390GD range, supplied pre-galvanized. The grade is not interchangeable: higher yield strength springs back more, so the same finished section needs different roller geometry and more compensation. It also changes how the perforated web behaves during forming. Send the grade with the drawing — the tooling is designed around it.

faq.q: Can you match the hole pattern of an existing rack system?
faq.a: Yes. The punching tooling is made to the pattern, and a sample profile or a dimensioned drawing is enough to reproduce it. One thing worth raising early: connector patterns are often the intellectual property of the rack system owner and some are protected. Deciding what you are entitled to produce is the buyer's call, not the machine builder's — we tool to the pattern you specify.

faq.q: Are beams produced the same way as uprights?
faq.a: No, and it is worth separating the two when you plan the investment. Uprights are open perforated sections and the whole line is built around punching accuracy. Beams are usually closed box sections, often formed from two profiles and joined, so the line carries a different station sequence and a joining stage instead of a large punching group. Most racking manufacturers end up with two lines rather than one that compromises on both.

features.text: Diamond/knurl embossing is pressed continuously in the roll forming stations.

features.title: Drainage and lightening holes
features.text: Hole patterns are punched in-line; the platform gets lighter and safer at once.

faq.a: Yes, the embossing and punching unit is integrated; the anti-slip pattern is formed on the plank surface while the profile is being rolled.

faq.q: How is plank length set?

yol-bariyeri.name: Guardrail Production Line
yol-bariyeri.metaTitle: Guardrail Roll Forming Machine: Highway W-Beam
yol-bariyeri.short: A heavy-duty roll forming line for W-beam guardrail profiles.
yol-bariyeri.hero: A heavy-duty line producing W-beam (two-wave) and three-wave guardrail profiles — the standard of road safety; it forms the wave profile in thick galvanized sheet with standard-compliant precision.
yol-bariyeri.meta: Guardrail production line: a heavy-duty roll forming solution for W-beam and three-wave highway barrier profiles.

features.title: Standard-compliant forming
features.text: Roll tooling design and form control for barrier geometries within EN 1317.

features.title: Heavy frame structure
features.text: A rigid body and strong drive keep 3-4 mm galvanized sheet running true even in the wave form.

features.title: Hole and length precision
features.text: Connection holes and cut lengths are fixed under servo control; on-site assembly is trouble-free.

process.title: Coil loading and decoiling
process.text: The coil is loaded onto a heavy-duty decoiler and gripped from the inside diameter by hydraulic expansion. Guardrail coils are wide and heavy, so a loading car and a pressure arm hold the outer wrap down — an unrestrained wrap on thick material can spring loose as the strip is drawn off.

process.title: Straightening
process.text: The coil set — the curvature the strip keeps from being wound — is taken out before any forming happens. This matters more on guardrail than on light profiles: residual bow left in a flat strip becomes visible once the wave is formed, and a beam that is not straight will not sit true against the posts on site.

process.title: Punching while flat
process.text: Bolt holes and post slots are punched before the strip reaches the forming stations. Punching a finished beam would distort the wave around the hole and leave the hole itself on a curved surface; punching flat keeps the hole pitch under servo control and the edges clean.

process.title: Progressive roll forming
process.text: The wave is not formed in one pass. Each station takes a share of the total angle so the material work-hardens gradually instead of thinning or cracking at the crests. Thick galvanized sheet needs a longer station sequence than a thin roofing profile for exactly this reason — the sequence is what protects the section, not the pressure.

process.title: Cut to length
process.text: Hydraulic cutting separates the beam in the formed section, with a die that matches the finished cross-section. A die that does not follow the wave pulls the section out of shape at the cut and leaves an edge that has to be reworked before galvanizing.

process.title: Run-out and stacking
process.text: Finished beams leave the line onto a run-out table and are stacked ready for galvanizing or for shipment. Handling matters here too: a beam dragged across another one scratches the surface, which on pre-galvanized material means a coating repair.

faq.q: Can I produce W-beam and thrie-beam on the same line?
faq.a: The two sections need different roller sets. Both can run on the same frame by changing the set; for frequent switching we recommend a quick-change arrangement.

faq.q: Is galvanized sheet processed, or is the profile galvanized afterwards?
faq.a: Both are possible. For pre-galvanized sheet the roller surface and pressure are set accordingly; for post-galvanizing the profile is rolled from bare steel.

faq.q: How are holes and mounting slots made?
faq.a: A hydraulic press unit is integrated into the line; connection holes and slots are punched before the profile leaves the line.

faq.q: Which standard applies to guardrail, and what does it require from the line?
faq.a: EN 1317 is the European standard for road restraint systems. It classifies barriers by containment level, impact severity and working width, and it tests the installed system as a whole — not the beam on its own. What that asks of the production line is repeatability: wave geometry, hole pitch and beam length have to stay within the tolerances of the approved drawing, so the system that was crash-tested is the same one coming off the line. The approval itself belongs to the barrier system owner; the line makes conformity producible, it does not carry the certificate.

faq.q: Which steel grade is used for the beams?
faq.a: Guardrail beams are normally rolled from structural steel in the S235 to S355 range, and which one depends on the containment class the system was approved at. The grade is not just a purchasing detail: a higher yield strength springs back more, so the same wave needs different roller geometry and more compensation. Send the grade and thickness with the enquiry — the roll tooling is designed around them, not adjusted to them afterwards.

faq.q: How does hot-dip galvanizing affect the line?
faq.a: There are two routes and they load the line differently. If the beam is galvanized after forming, which is the common route for highway work under EN ISO 1461, the line rolls bare steel and the zinc is applied at a galvanizing plant — the coating then covers the cut edges and the punched holes as well. If pre-galvanized coil is used, the coating is already on the strip, so roller surfaces and pressures are set to avoid scratching it, and the cut and punched edges stay uncoated. Which route applies is normally fixed by the project specification rather than by the machine.

faq.q: How long does a changeover between profiles take?
faq.a: Moving between W-beam and thrie-beam means changing the roller set; the frame, drive and punching unit stay where they are. How long that takes depends on how the line was built for it — a standard arrangement makes it a planned job between production runs, while a cassette or quick-change design brings it down considerably. If you expect to alternate between the two sections regularly, say so at the enquiry stage: designing the frame for it costs far less than retrofitting it later.

faq.q: Can guardrail posts be produced on the same line?
faq.a: No. Sigma and C-section posts are a different cross-section with a different station sequence and a different cutting arrangement, so they run on their own roll forming line. We build both, and when a project needs beams and posts together the two lines are quoted as a set — which is usually the more sensible way to buy them, because the post length and hole pattern have to match the beam they carry.

gurultu-bariyeri.name: Noise Barrier Production Line
gurultu-bariyeri.short: A roll forming line for sound barrier cassette and panel profiles.
gurultu-bariyeri.hero: A line producing the aluminium/steel cassette profiles of noise barriers along highways and railways; perforated front (absorber) and closed back panels can be produced on the same line platform.
gurultu-bariyeri.meta: Noise barrier production line: a roll forming solution producing perforated and solid sound barrier cassette and panel profiles.

features.title: Perforated panel production
features.text: Front-face perforation for acoustic absorption is integrated in-line or before feeding.

features.title: Aluminium and steel compatibility
features.text: Roll pressure settings for different materials and thicknesses are managed with recipes.

features.title: Long panel capability
features.text: Precise cut-to-length and safe stacking for barrier module lengths.

process.title: Coil loading and decoiling
process.text: Noise barrier panels are a visible product on a road, and both aluminium and coated steel show every handling mark. The coil is loaded and guided so the face never rubs, and where the coil carries a protective film it is kept on through forming and taken off only after the panel is stacked.

process.title: Straightening
process.text: The strip is flattened before it reaches the perforation station. This is not only about the finished panel being straight: a strip that still holds coil curvature does not sit flat under the punch, and a perforation punched into a curved sheet comes out with uneven hole edges and a burr that varies across the width.

process.title: Perforation of the absorbing face
process.text: The front sheet is perforated flat, to the pattern the acoustic design calls for. What matters acoustically is hole diameter together with open area ratio, and both are set by the acoustic engineer rather than by the machine — the line's job is to reproduce that pattern identically panel after panel, because a varying open area means a barrier whose absorption varies along the road.

process.title: Keeping the bend zones solid
process.text: The perforated field has to stop short of every line the profile will later be bent on. Forming through a perforated zone tears the material at the holes and takes the stiffness out of exactly the edge that carries the panel in its post. So the perforation tool and the forming stations are phased together — the pattern is positioned relative to the finished section, not simply centred on the strip.

process.title: Roll forming to material
process.text: Aluminium and steel do not run the same way. Aluminium is softer and picks up on the rollers, so it needs lower pressure, different roller surfaces and attention to lubrication; steel takes more pressure and springs back more. The line holds both as recipes rather than being re-set by hand each time the order changes.

process.title: Cut to length and stacking
process.text: Panels are cut to the module length the barrier layout uses, which is set by the post spacing on the project. Finished panels are stacked with the face protected — a scratch on an absorbing panel is not just cosmetic on aluminium, it is where corrosion starts on coated steel.

faq.q: Are the perforated front panel and cassette back panel made on one line?
faq.a: They are two different sections, so two roller sets are normally used. For the perforated panel the punching unit is integrated into the line.

faq.q: Does the hole pattern affect acoustic performance?
faq.a: Yes; hole diameter and open area ratio directly determine sound absorption. We tool and produce the pattern defined in your acoustic design.

faq.q: Can you produce aluminium panels?
faq.a: Yes. Aluminium requires lower pressure and a different roller surface; the line is set up for the material.

faq.q: Which standards govern noise barriers, and what part of them concerns the line?
faq.a: Road traffic noise reducing devices are placed on the market under EN 14388, with EN 1793 covering acoustic performance — sound absorption and airborne sound insulation — and EN 1794 the non-acoustic side such as wind load, stone impact and safety in the event of collision. Almost all of that is tested on the finished device, not on the sheet: the cassette with its perforated face, absorbing core and back panel behaves as a system. What the line is responsible for is producing the metalwork to the design consistently, so that the barrier installed is the one that was tested.

faq.q: Does the perforation pattern really change acoustic performance?
faq.a: Yes, and it is one of the few things on the panel where a small production drift has an audible result. Absorption depends on hole diameter and open area ratio together with what sits behind the sheet. If open area varies between production runs, the barrier absorbs differently along its length while looking identical. This is why the pattern comes from the acoustic design as a fixed specification and the line reproduces it rather than approximating it.

faq.q: Why can't the sheet be perforated all the way to the edge?
faq.a: Because the edges are where the panel is bent and where it carries load. A perforation running into a bend line tears at the holes as the section is formed, and the flange that should hold the panel in its post ends up weakened exactly where it matters. The perforated field is therefore laid out relative to the finished profile, with solid material left at every bend and at the ends. It is a common point of confusion when a panel is being copied from a sample — the visible perforated area is smaller than the sheet.

faq.q: What changes on the line between aluminium and steel?
faq.a: Aluminium is softer, marks more easily and tends to pick up on roller surfaces, so it runs at lower pressure with different roller surfaces and more attention to lubrication. Steel takes higher pressure and springs back more, which means different roller geometry for the same finished section. Both can run on one line, but they are set up as separate recipes; if you expect to alternate between them regularly, say so at the enquiry stage so the roller sets are planned for it.

faq.q: Does the line also assemble the cassette and fill the absorbing core?
faq.a: No. The roll forming line produces the perforated front profile and the closed back profile. Inserting the mineral wool or other absorbing core, closing the cassette and fitting the end caps is a separate assembly operation with its own equipment. It is worth planning the two together, because the cassette design determines the profile geometry — but they are not the same machine and should be budgeted separately.

trapez-cephe-paneli.name: Trapezoidal Sheet and Facade Panel Line
trapez-cephe-paneli.short: Forming, cut-to-length and stacking for roofing and cladding profiles.
trapez-cephe-paneli.hero: Lines for trapezoidal sheet, standing-seam roofing profile and facade panel used in roofing and cladding. Two things decide this family: flatness across a wide sheet, and getting a painted surface through forming undamaged.
trapez-cephe-paneli.meta: Production lines for trapezoidal sheet, standing-seam roofing and facade cladding profiles: forming, cut-to-length, automatic stacking and packing.

features.title: Flatness across a wide sheet
features.text: Cladding profiles are wide and thin, so a flatness error shows immediately on installation; a levelling unit is effectively mandatory in this family.

features.title: Forming suited to a coated surface
features.text: Painted and galvanised sheet keeps its coating when the section is built up in stages; roll station count is chosen accordingly.

features.title: Stacking and packing
features.text: Cladding profiles go to site in packs, so the line ends with an automatic stacking and packing unit.

faq.q: Does forming damage the coating on painted sheet?
faq.a: Not with the right roll design and surface hardness. The station count is what decides it: build the section in stages rather than in one step and the material is not forced. Since the coating will sit outdoors on the finished product, this is directly a question of service life — we ask for the sheet's coating type at quotation stage.

faq.q: How long does changing the profile section take?
faq.a: Changing the section means changing the roll tooling, which is a different job from changing the length. Cut length is servo controlled and called from the recipe, so it changes while the line runs. How long a section change takes depends on whether the tooling is built on the line or off it in a cassette.

c-sigma-omega.metaTitle: C Purlin Roll Forming Machine: C, Sigma & Omega

features.text: C, Sigma and Omega forms are produced on the same line with adjustable stations, lowering the investment cost.

process.title: Coil loading and decoiling
process.text: Structural sections are usually rolled from pre-galvanized coil in a range of thicknesses, because the same line serves purlins, studs and framing members that are specified differently. The decoiler is sized for the heaviest coil the line will see rather than the average one — a decoiler chosen for the typical order becomes the bottleneck the first time a heavy job arrives.

process.title: Straightening
process.text: Coil set comes out before anything else. On structural profiles this is what decides whether the finished member is straight along its length: C and Sigma sections are asymmetric, so any curvature left in the strip does not simply stay as a gentle bow — it combines with the forming and comes out as twist, which is far harder to correct afterwards than a simple bend.

process.title: Punching to the structural pattern
process.text: Service holes, bolt holes and web openings are punched flat, in the pattern the structural design specifies. Position matters more than it does on a cladding profile: a hole in the web of a loaded member is a designed feature, and moving it is a structural decision rather than a production convenience.

process.title: Adjustable roll forming
process.text: This is what separates this line from a single-profile one. The roll groups adjust so that section width and height change without stripping the machine down, which is how three families of section share one line. The trade-off is worth understanding: an adjustable line covers a range, a dedicated line runs one section faster. Which one is right depends on how varied your order book actually is.

process.title: Flying shear
process.text: Cutting happens on the move, so the line does not stop for every piece. On structural work orders tend to be long lists of mixed lengths rather than one length repeated, so the time lost to stopping and restarting adds up quickly over a shift.

process.title: Stacking
process.text: Finished sections are collected and stacked. Long structural members are easy to damage between the line and the truck, and a bent flange on a purlin is not a cosmetic problem — it is a member that will not sit flat against the rafter it bolts to.

faq.q: Is it possible to run all three sections on one line?
faq.a: Yes, with a cassette-change configuration C, sigma and omega run on the same frame. The more sections you run, the faster a quick-change arrangement pays for itself.

faq.q: What is needed when the profile height changes?
faq.a: With an adjustable cassette structure the height is selected on the panel; if the section family changes, the roller set is swapped.

faq.q: How long do the rollers last?
faq.a: Rollers are made from 4140 steel and hardened to 58-60 Rockwell; with correct pressure settings they can produce millions of metres of profile.

faq.q: Where is the real limit of an adjustable line?
faq.a: The adjustment covers a range of widths and heights within one section family and the geometry it was designed around. What it does not do is turn one profile family into another: moving between C, Sigma and Omega is a roller set matter, and moving outside the designed range means new tooling regardless of how much adjustment the machine has. The honest way to specify a line like this is to give the full list of sections you expect to produce, including the ones you do not have orders for yet, and let the range be designed around that list.

faq.q: Why does twist matter more than bow on structural sections?
faq.a: Because a bow can often be pulled out during erection and a twist cannot. C and Sigma sections are asymmetric about at least one axis, so residual stress left in the strip does not release as a simple curve — it releases as a rotation along the length. A twisted purlin will not sit flat where it bolts, and the fix on site is usually to reject the piece. This is why the straightening stage carries more weight on a structural line than most buyers expect, and why it is worth asking about specifically.

faq.q: Can hole patterns be changed without new tooling?
faq.a: Hole position and spacing are recipe values, so a new layout is a data change rather than a tooling change. Hole shape and size are tooling — a different diameter or a slot instead of a round hole means a punch and die. When you plan the line, it is worth listing every hole shape you use across your product range at the start, because adding shapes later is a purchase each time while adding positions is free.

faq.q: How long do the roll tools last?
faq.a: Longer than most people expect, and it depends much more on what runs through them than on hours. Uncoated steel, abrasive coatings, thick material and tight radii all wear tooling faster than light galvanized sheet at generous radii. Rolls are a maintenance item rather than a consumable — they are re-machined rather than replaced when they eventually go out of tolerance. What actually kills a roll set early is running it misaligned or under too much pressure, which is a setup discipline question more than a metallurgy one.

faq.q: Is one adjustable line better than two dedicated lines?
faq.a: It depends on the mix, and it is worth doing the arithmetic rather than assuming. An adjustable line wins when the order book is varied and no single section dominates — you buy one machine, one control system and one set of spares, and changeovers are frequent but short. Two dedicated lines win when two sections make up most of the volume, because each runs at its own optimum with no changeover at all. If one section is more than roughly half your output, dedicating a line to it usually pays.

rulo-acicilar.short: Hydraulic 6-20 t and mechanical 500-2,500 kg decoiling solutions.

features.title: Hydraulic mandrel expansion
features.text: On heavy-duty series the coil inner diameter is clamped hydraulically; loading is fast and safe.

faq.q: What is the difference between hydraulic and mechanical decoilers?
faq.a: The mechanical series carries 500–2500 kg coils on a handwheel-tightened mandrel; the hydraulic series reaches 6–20 tons with hydraulic mandrel expansion and braking. For heavy coils and high line speeds, hydraulic is the safe choice.

faq.q: What capacity should I choose?
faq.a: Leave one step of margin above your heaviest coil: 6 tons for a 5-ton coil, 10 tons for an 8-ton coil. We verify the choice against coil width and inner diameter (450–560 mm) together.

faq.q: What does bidirectional operation provide?
faq.a: Since the shaft rotates both ways, the strip can be fed from the top or the bottom — you handle coils wound in either direction without changing your line layout.

faq.q: When is a loading car necessary?
faq.a: Mounting heavy coils onto the shaft with a forklift is risky and slow; a hydraulic loading car aligns the coil and seats it on the mandrel in seconds. We recommend it as standard above 6 tons.

faq.q: What is an uncoiler, and is it the same as a decoiler?
faq.a: They are the same machine. Uncoiler, decoiler and coil reel are used interchangeably — uncoiler is the more common term in North America, decoiler in Europe. Both describe the unit that holds the coil at the head of the line and pays the strip off under controlled tension. Everything on this page applies whichever word you searched for.

faq.q: What is the working principle of a decoiler machine?
faq.a: The coil is seated on a mandrel that expands against its inner diameter, so it is gripped from the inside rather than clamped from the outside. As the line draws strip, the mandrel turns and a brake holds back-tension so the coil cannot overrun and loosen. On the hydraulic series both the expansion and the braking are powered; on the mechanical series the mandrel is tightened by handwheel and the shaft runs under speed control with a brake system.

faq.q: Do you supply manual decoilers?
faq.a: The mechanical series is what is usually meant by a manual decoiler: the mandrel is tightened by handwheel rather than hydraulically, and coil tension is held by a brake with speed control. It covers coils from 500 to 2,500 kg. Above that the hydraulic series takes over, where mandrel expansion and braking are both powered and a loading car handles seating the coil.

faq.q: Can decoiling, straightening and feeding be combined in one machine?
faq.a: Yes — that is what a compact line is: decoiler, straightener and servo feeder on a single platform, managed from one HMI, for shops without the floor space for a classic layout. Where coils are heavy or the line layout is already fixed, a separate decoiler feeding a straightener servo feeder is the better arrangement.

faq.q: What determines the feeding pitch accuracy?
faq.a: The servo motor–gearbox pair, the pressure of the Ø85 mm feed rollers and synchronization with the press cam. Settings are stored as recipes; with 250-die memory, no readjustment is needed after a die change.

faq.q: What material range does it handle?
faq.a: 0.4–4.0 mm thickness and strip widths up to 1600 mm, with a free feeding speed of 35 m/min. For material outside this range we size the line together with you.

faq.q: When is the mini series sufficient?
faq.a: For narrow strip and small presses, the mini series saves floor space and cost; pitch accuracy is identical to the standard series. Strip width and coil weight define the limits.

faq.q: How is press synchronization set up?
faq.a: The press cam signal is wired to the feeder; feeding is timed to the press dead center and a pilot-pin release is applied. Our team performs commissioning on site.

faq.q: What is a servo feeder?
faq.a: A servo feeder is the machine that advances strip into the die between press strokes. A servo motor drives the feed rolls, so the length of each advance is a number in the control rather than something fixed by mechanical linkage — that is what makes it repeatable to the millimetre and changeable between jobs without retooling. The drive here is Schneider Lexium, running 2 × Ø85 mm feed rolls from a 7-inch touchscreen.

faq.q: What are the three types of press feeder?
faq.a: Air, mechanical and servo. Air feeders are the simplest and suit short, light work. Mechanical feeders take their motion from the press itself, so feed length is set by the linkage and changing it means changing hardware. Servo feeders drive the rolls independently, which is why the pitch is set in the control instead of on the machine. The trade-off between the last two is worked through on the servo versus mechanical feeding comparison.

faq.q: When do I need a straightener servo feeder?
faq.a: If coil set and curvature in the strip are degrading part quality, combining feeding and straightening in one frame saves both floor space and investment.

faq.q: How many straightening rollers should I choose?
faq.a: Thin and surface-critical sheets need more rollers, thick sheets fewer. We help you pick the right variant among 7 / 9 / 11 / 13 rollers for your material.

faq.q: How does it differ from a separate straightener and feeder?
faq.a: One frame, one control, one operator panel: the synchronization problem between two machines disappears, the line gets shorter, wiring and commissioning become simpler.

faq.q: How is the straightening pressure adjusted?
faq.a: Pressure is set according to sheet thickness and stored in the recipe; the SCHNEIDER touchscreen keeps up to 250 die memories. It works up to 0.5–4 mm thickness and 1600 mm width.

faq.q: Is this the same as a decoiler straightener feeder?
faq.a: Close, but not the same machine. A decoiler straightener feeder combines all three functions in one unit; this one combines the last two — straightening and feeding — in a single body and takes its strip from a separate decoiler. Where all three need to sit on one platform, that is a compact line.

otomatik-istifleyici.name: Automatic Stacker
otomatik-istifleyici.metaTitle: Automatic Stacker Machine for Sheet Metal Lines
otomatik-istifleyici.short: Stacks the profile leaving the line — unattended, square and counted.
otomatik-istifleyici.hero: The last link in a roll forming or cut-to-length line: a unit that collects the cut profile or sheet at line speed and stacks it in pack order. Manual stacking is the step that most limits line speed and most raises the risk of damage; automatic stacking removes that bottleneck.
otomatik-istifleyici.meta: Automatic stacking unit for roll forming and cut-to-length lines: collection at line speed, counted packs, unattended operation.

features.text: Stacking runs to the line's output tempo, so the line never has to slow down or wait for the stack.

features.title: Counted packs
features.text: Pieces per pack come from the recipe; counting is not left to the operator and the pack leaves ready to ship.

features.title: Surface protection
features.text: The profile is placed rather than dragged into position, which lowers the risk of scratching on parts with a visible face.

faq.q: Can it be added to a line I already have?
faq.a: In most cases yes, but two things decide it: the line's discharge height, and whether the cutting unit can give a signal. The stacker needs a trigger from the cut to know when to move; if the control system cannot expose that signal, an intermediate solution is built. The layout also has to leave clear floor space on the pick-up side for a forklift or pallet truck.

faq.q: Will the same stacker handle different profile sections?
faq.a: As long as the section family is similar, yes — the setting changes with the recipe. But profiles with very different width-to-height ratios (a narrow rail versus a wide trapezoidal sheet, say) do not work well on the same holding arrangement. Telling us up front which profile families will run on the line lets us pick the right arrangement.

faq.q: How is tolerance held on small sections?
faq.a: On a small section the problem is not force but repeatability. Roll count and station spacing are chosen so the section builds up in stages; thin material forced in one step springs back and the dimension drifts across the shift. A levelling unit is not optional here either.

faq.q: Is there a risk of scratching painted or coated sheet?
faq.a: With the right roll surface and feeding arrangement, it is close to nil. On parts with a visible face, what matters is that the profile travels carried rather than dragged along the line; automatic stacking at the exit is preferred for the same reason.

faq.q: Does forming damage the coating on galvanised sheet?

faq.q: Why is feed accuracy so decisive in series production?
faq.a: The press has to find the sheet in the same position on every stroke. If the position drifts, the part dimension drifts with it and the die is loaded on one side, which raises both scrap and tool wear. In high-volume production a small deviation turns into a large number by the end of the day.

faq.q: Can a complete feeding line fit into a tight footprint?
faq.a: Yes — decoiler, straightener and servo feeder can be combined on a single platform. That is exactly what the compact line exists for: it shrinks the floor space that three separately placed machines would occupy.

sustain.metaTitle: Sustainability: Scrap, Energy and Data-Led Production
sustain.metaDesc: Servosteel's approach to sustainability: cutting scrap through line yield, energy draw with servo drives, production data and remote support.
sustain.title: For us, sustainability is what the machine does
sustain.desc: A machine builder's environmental effect shows up not in its own factory but in what the line it sold does at a customer's plant over thirty years. That is where we read it: sheet not wasted, electricity not drawn, journeys not made.
sustain.approachTitle: Not a reporting heading — four measurable items
sustain.approachText: You will not find a carbon emission figure on this page, because writing an unverified number is worse than writing none. Instead we set out the four items that make a difference on every shift the line runs, and why they work. Three of them land in your cost sheet as well; in this business sustainability and efficiency point the same way.

pillars.title: Scrap: the largest item
pillars.text: Every tonne of sheet that goes to scrap is a tonne that has to be made again — melting, rolling and transport included. Raising line yield is therefore the most direct environmental intervention there is. When the master coil width does not divide exactly by the strip width, the remainder becomes scrap: cutting 120 mm strips from a 1,250 mm coil with 10 mm edge trim comes to 4 %. A better strip plan brings that down.

pillars.title: Energy: a servo draws only while it moves
pillars.text: Mechanical feeding systems turn continuously for as long as the line runs. A servo drive draws power while feeding and not while waiting. The difference is proportional to how much of the shift is spent idle — pronounced in stop-start production, smaller in continuous running. Which is why the gain has to be discussed against your own shift pattern.

pillars.title: Data: what is not measured is not improved
pillars.text: Production reporting shows how long the line actually ran, where it stopped and what it produced per shift. Scrap and downtime only come down once they are counted. Data collection and reporting run over the HMI on our lines — you can see it in the video below.

pillars.title: Service life and remote support
pillars.text: Long-lived rolls and knife sets mean fewer spare parts have to be manufactured. Remote diagnosis, meanwhile, removes a large share of the cases that would otherwise require a visit: every flight and every road trip not taken is an emission genuinely saved.

We have collected six concrete ways to bring scrap down in <article>a separate article</article> — measured across annual tonnage, this item is larger than the price of the line itself in most plants.

sustain.proofText: We can describe data collection and reporting as a system installed on the line rather than as a goal. The videos below show production reporting over the HMI and a structural profile line running.

goals.text: We aim to increase the time and budget we put into R&D. Every problem that comes back from the field becomes a design input for the next line.
